lessons.title: 1990 to today: the quality turn and the boutiques
lessons.body:
Turkey's wine industry as we know it began in the early 1990s. Two old houses turned towards quality, and a few wealthy newcomers founded small estates with their own vineyards. Once the state monopoly ended, the number of producers grew several times over, and many of them were boutiques. Then in 2013 a new law banned alcohol advertising and promotion and restricted retail sales. Wineries have been working out how to sell under that rule ever since.

### Where things stood around 1990

Lesson 3 left the industry dominated by the state's Tekel wineries and the two big private houses, Doluca and Kavaklıdere. For most of the twentieth century the industry was led by the marketing and sales of those two companies, according to [Wikipedia's summary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkish_wine). Wine was a bulk product, mostly sold under brand names rather than grape or place.

The economist Durmuş Özdemir counted only 12 wine producers in 2000 (Lesson 3). That small number is the base everything below grew from.

### The quality turn: three first moves

A **boutique winery** (*butik şaraphane*) here means a small, usually privately owned producer that grows much of its own fruit and sells on quality rather than volume. A **varietal wine** is one labelled by its grape, such as "Cabernet Sauvignon" or "Öküzgözü", instead of by a brand alone.

| Who | When | What changed | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Doluca | early 1990s | Fine wines from international grapes; the Sarafin label pioneered varietal branding | [Decanter](https://www.decanter.com/wine/turkey-wine-lands-on-the-rise-535193/); [Wikipedia list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_wineries_in_Turkey) |
| Kavaklıdere | early 1990s | Quality wines from native Öküzgözü, Boğazkere and Kalecik Karası | [Decanter](https://www.decanter.com/wine/turkey-wine-lands-on-the-rise-535193/) |
| Gülor | 1993 | Founded by Güler Sabancı; often called the first boutique winery | [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkish_wine) |

The Turkish wine expert Levon Bağış calls the Doluca and Kavaklıdere moves the milestones of the modern story (Decanter, Lesson 1). Wikipedia adds that the first boutiques planted their own vineyards with international varieties to make varietally labelled estate wines, and that regulatory changes in the 1990s opened the door for them.

### The boutique wave of the 2000s

Privatisation took Tekel out of wine production by 2004 (Lesson 3), and the field opened. Many new wineries were small, family-run estates, and several worked with foreign consultants ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkish_wine)). Three examples show the range:

- **Paşaeli** (2000) set out to rescue endangered native grapes ([Wikipedia list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_wineries_in_Turkey)).
- **Corvus** (2002) was founded on the island of Bozcaada by Reşit Söley, an architect by training ([Oxford Business Group](https://oxfordbusinessgroup.com/reports/turkey/2015-report/economy/upon-a-time-history-and-viticulture-beckon-visitors-to-a-small-treasure-offshore)).
- **Urlice** began selling wine commercially in 2006, one of the first of the new Urla producers ([Lonely Planet](https://www.lonelyplanet.com/articles/turkey-urla-izmir-turkish-wine-on-the-map)).

The founders fit the pattern Lesson 1 described: people who made money elsewhere and put it into land and a cellar.

How fast did the number grow? Sources count differently, so the figures below are not one series.

| Year | Producers | What is counted | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2000 | 12 | Wine producers | Özdemir (Lesson 3) |
| 2002 | about 40 | Wine producers | [Bloomberg HT column](https://www.bloomberght.com/yorum/irfan-donat/2317333-uzumde-kacan-milyar-dolarlik-firsat) |
| 2003 | 47 | Registered fermented-drink producers, mostly wine | [Wine Business International](https://www.wine-business-international.com/wine/general/dark-market-turkey) |
| 2012 | 157 | Same definition | Wine Business International |
| recent | 174 | Wine businesses, making 82 million litres | [Çukurova University review, 2023](https://avesis.cu.edu.tr/yayin/c11c2a9b-a7bf-424a-a5ff-fd751def7376/turk-sarapciliginin-durumu-ve-sorunlari) |

The early counts disagree because some include all fermented drinks and some count licences rather than active wineries. I take the trend from the 47-to-157 pair, because it uses one definition across a decade. The direction is clear either way: roughly a tenfold rise in about 20 years.

The same Bloomberg HT column says only five or six producers make more than a million litres a year, so most of the roughly 200 it counts are boutiques. The output figure also varies: Lesson 1 used Falstaff's 60 million litres, while the Çukurova review gives 82 million. The review also puts capacity use at about 50%, meaning the industry built more cellar space than it fills.

### Native grapes come back

The first boutiques planted mostly international grapes. The next step was native ones. A project called Heritage Vines of Türkiye has worked on this. Its co-founder Sabiha Apaydın Gönenli told [Decanter](https://www.decanter.com/wine/turkey-wine-lands-on-the-rise-535193/) that about 20 local varieties were in commercial use when it began, and that the number is now 65. I found no independent count, so treat that as the project's own figure. Urla Karası, a red that had almost disappeared, is one rescued grape. Lessons 7 and 8 cover the grapes themselves.

### 2013: Law 6487

In 2013 parliament amended the alcohol rules with Law No. 6487. It came into force in June 2013 ([The Citizen](https://citizen.co.za/news/news-world/turkey-wine-culture-food-drink-religion-lifestyle)). Its main provisions, from contemporary press reports:

1. **Advertising and promotion ban.** Drink companies may not promote their brands, and images of alcohol are blurred on television ([Times of Israel, AP](https://www.timesofisrael.com/turkey-passes-law-restricting-alcohol-sales/)). Trademarks, logos and slogans of alcoholic drinks may not appear in advertising ([World Trademark Review](https://www.worldtrademarkreview.com/article/new-legislation-have-significant-impact-trademarks-alcoholic-beverages)).
2. **Night-time retail ban.** Shops may not sell alcohol between 22:00 and 06:00. This took effect on 9 September 2013 and does not apply to bars, restaurants or clubs ([Eurasianet](https://eurasianet.org/turkey-taking-the-11th-step-toward-prohibition)).
3. **Distance rule.** No sales near mosques and schools, generally reported as within 100 metres. Reports differ on scope; Eurasianet says it applies to new licences only, and I follow that.

The government presented the law as protecting public health and young people; critics saw it as part of a conservative religious agenda (same sources). For wineries, the promotion ban mattered most. Producers said it ruled out tastings, events and newspaper advertising, and one Bozcaada vintner estimated his business shrank by 5 to 10% in the following months ([Tengri News](https://en.tengrinews.kz/news/22749/)). Ali Basman, head of the Turkish Wine Producers Association, said it is hard to sell wine without being able to explain the winery, and that the industry would have to export more.

### After 2013: the rules kept tightening

Law 6487 was not the last step. Selling alcohol online is not allowed ([The Citizen](https://citizen.co.za/news/news-world/turkey-wine-culture-food-drink-religion-lifestyle)). In 2024 producers were required to post a collateral deposit of 5 million to 50 million lira against future tax fines ([Wein.plus](https://magazine.wein.plus/news/turkey-government-demands-enormous-sums-from-wineries-alcohol-sales-in-turkey-to-be-further-restricted)). In June 2026 an omnibus law banned alcohol brand names and logos from shops, bars and restaurants, with retailers given until 20 June 2027 to comply ([EUCAM](https://eucam.info/2026/06/22/turkey-bans-alcohol-names-logos-and-packaging-images-in-shops-events-and-sponsored-content/)) Parliament also barred alcohol producers from sponsoring events under their brand.

The industry organised around these limits. The trade body Wines of Turkey was set up in 2008 by leading wineries to build the home market and exports ([Wines of Turkey](https://winesofturkey.org/about/)). The Thrace Vineyard Route (*Trakya Bağ Rotası*), Turkey's first, was created in 2013 with a grant from the regional development agency and 12 boutique wineries ([BirGün](https://www.birgun.net/makale/agro-turizm-baglar-gastronomi-ve-sarap-260264)). Routes let a region bring visitors to the cellar door, which is one of the few channels the ban leaves open. Lesson 17 covers them.

### What this means if you look at it as a business

This section is my reading, not a sourced claim.

- **The boutique boom was financed by outside wealth, not by wine profits.** Founders with money from other industries could carry years of losses. That still sets the entry ticket.
- **2013 changed the cost of selling more than the cost of making.** A boutique cannot buy awareness, so it must earn it through visits, sommeliers, awards and word of mouth. Hospitality on the estate becomes a sales channel, not a side business.
- **Half-empty cellars mean spare capacity is cheap to find.** With capacity use around 50% and contract production banned since 2009 (Lesson 1), owners of idle cellars have an incentive to sell or lease whole facilities rather than wine.
- **Regulatory risk is now a line item.** Collateral rules and logo bans arrive with little warning. A business plan here needs a buffer for rule changes, as it would for weather.

### Key terms

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| butik şaraphane | Boutique winery: small, privately owned, quality-focused, usually with its own vineyards |
| varietal wine | A wine labelled by its grape variety |
| estate wine | Wine made from a producer's own vineyards |
| Law 6487 | The 2013 law banning alcohol promotion and restricting retail sales |
| reklam yasağı | Advertising ban |
| Trakya Bağ Rotası | Thrace Vineyard Route, Turkey's first wine route (2013) |
| Wines of Turkey | Trade body of leading wineries, founded 2008 |
| capacity use | Share of installed production capacity actually used |

The 2013 promotion ban and the first vineyard route in Thrace

quiz.why: Both milestones are the early-1990s quality turns at the two old houses. The 1926 and 1929 founding dates are tempting, but those firms made mostly bulk wine for decades before the turn.

quiz.why: The lesson defines a boutique by size, private ownership, own vineyards and a quality focus. Licensing date is tempting because many are recent, but age is not the definition; Gülor dates from 1993.

news.headline: 後継者難倒産、年度上半期として過去最多の263件。
news.body: 東京商工リサーチによると、4〜9月の後継者難倒産は前年同期比23.4%増。代表者の死亡（120件）と体調不良（105件）で85.5%を占め、資本金1千万円未満が68.4%でした。
news.why: 2年続いた減少が止まり、再び増加に転じました。TSR自身も、事業継続か譲渡か廃業かを経営者が早く決断する必要があると結論づけています。

news.headline: 1〜6月の後継者難倒産も過去最多の264件。
news.body: 96.2%が破産でした。
news.why: 倒産した後に再建される会社はほとんどありません。引き継ぐ機会があるのは倒産の前です。

news.headline: 佐嘉酒造が全面リニューアルを完了。
news.body: 福岡の地域みらいグループ傘下で330年余りの歴史を持つ佐嘉酒造が、3年がかりで5棟を新築しました。
news.why: 古い蔵を引き継いだ地域企業が、維持にとどまらず大きく投資した例です。

news.headline: ベストアメニティが老舗酒蔵「花の露」を承継。
news.body: 食品会社のベストアメニティが福岡の老舗酒蔵を承継したと報じられました（有料記事のため見出しのみ確認）。
news.why: 食品・飲料の会社が酒蔵の買い手として定着しつつあります。

news.headline: 経産省の研究会が伝統的工芸品を取り上げる。
news.body: エンタメ・クリエイティブ政策研究会が、伝統的工芸品をアニメやファッション、デザインと並ぶ産業として位置づけました。
news.why: 政策の重心が、工芸の保存から、他の日本発コンテンツと組み合わせた海外展開へ移りつつあります。

news.headline: 帝国データバンクの集計で、2026年度上半期の後継者難倒産が296件となり、上半期として過去最多になりました。
news.body: 前年同期の264件から12.1%増で、集計を始めた2013年度以降で最多です。同社は通年で600件前後になると見込んでいます。業歴100年以上の老舗の倒産も88件（前年同期比23.9%増）でした。
news.why: 同じ期間を東京商工リサーチは263件と集計しており、調査会社によって数字が違います。どちらも増加という方向は一致しています。

news.headline: 業歴100年超の老舗企業の倒産が、1〜8月で112件となり、過去最多のペースで推移しています。
news.body: これまでの最多は2024年の146件で、2026年は年間160件を上回るペースです。業種別では製造業34件、卸売業24件、小売業22件で、後継者難や物価高が背景とされています。
news.why: 老舗は家の仕組みで長く続いてきた会社ですが、承継と収益の両方の圧力で退出が増えています。

news.headline: 和菓子店の倒産が1〜9月で22件となり、過去最多だった2025年を上回るペースです。
news.body: 2020年以降の和菓子店の倒産138件のうち、業歴100年以上が24件（17.4%）でした。原材料高に加え、菓子職人の高齢化で技術の承継が難しくなり、生産量を保てない店も出ています。
news.why: 技能を持つ職人の引退が事業の継続を左右する点で、酒蔵や伝統工芸と同じ構造を持つ業種です。

news.headline: 東京商工リサーチが、法人版事業承継税制の活用状況と特例承継計画の提出期限延長をまとめました。
news.body: 特例承継計画の提出は2023年度の5,546件から2025年度は2,264件に減り、提出期限は2026年3月末から2027年9月30日に延びました。一方、特例の適用を受ける贈与・相続の期限は2027年12月31日のままです。1〜8月の後継者難倒産は355件で前年同期比17.1%増でした。
news.why: 相続税・贈与税の納税猶予が全額になる特例の期限が近づいており、株式の承継を考える会社には時間の制約になります。税金は免除ではなく猶予で、取り消されれば利子税と合わせて納める必要がある点も押さえておくべきです。

news.headline: 非上場株の相続評価の見直しについて、知っている企業は36.6%にとどまるという東京商工リサーチの調査が出ました。
news.body: 10月1〜8日に5,257社が回答しました。見直しを知る企業のうち56.2%が評価額は「上昇しそう」と答え、中小企業では57.1%でした。国税庁は2026年4月から有識者会議を開いており、経済産業省・中小企業庁は9月16日に慎重な検証を求める意見を出しています。
news.why: 自社株の評価が上がれば、親族への承継で相続税・贈与税の負担が増えます。承継の費用と時期を左右する論点として、第7回（お金の問題）にも関わります。

news.headline: Endo Kazutoshi due to open a 10-seat omakase restaurant in Chelsea.
news.body: Endo Chelsea has a listening bar upstairs. His White City restaurant remains closed after a fire.
news.why: The top end of Japanese dining in London is Japanese-led and still expanding. His group also plans a second Sumi in Marylebone this year.

news.headline: Nakimushi opens in a three-storey Notting Hill townhouse.
news.body: It has ramen downstairs and a broader Japanese menu above, and comes from the team behind Dorian.
news.why: British restaurateurs keep moving into Japanese formats, here by combining two successful pop-ups.

news.headline: The BBC reports a Japan travel craze among young Britons.
news.body: The report put it down to social media and the weak yen.
news.why: The boom is now mainstream news, which usually means the early-adopter phase is over.

news.headline: Hyper Japan runs at Olympia London.
news.body: Last year's festival drew 53,000 visitors.
news.why: This year's attendance is the figure to look for.

news.headline: VisitBritain forecasts 276,000 visits from Japan this year, up 18%.
news.body: It hosted Japanese tour operators around England.
news.why: The reverse flow is recovering, but from a much lower base than the outbound one.

news.headline: Japan's tourism agency appoints FINN Partners for UK marketing.
news.body: The agency will run its UK public relations and marketing.
news.why: The brief is to push repeat visitors to lesser-known regions, which is where new travel products will be wanted.

news.headline: Wagamama starts taking table bookings for the first time in its 34-year history.
news.body: The walk-in-only chain now accepts same-day and advance bookings for groups of any size through OpenTable, its website and app; groups of 20 or more book by phone. The company says the change followed a trial and guest requests, and is pushing it with a festive set menu at £23 for two courses.
news.why: The UK's largest Japanese-inspired chain is giving up a format rule it has kept since 1992, a sign that casual dining now competes on convenience and occasion bookings, not just on queue-and-eat.

news.headline: Zadie's, billed as Manchester's first Itameshi (Japanese-Italian) restaurant, opens at Medlock Square in East Manchester.
news.body: The venue has 258 covers plus 30 counter seats and was developed with Gorgeous Group; the head chef previously worked at Zuma and Lucky Cat. It sits in a £300m hospitality development in East Manchester.
news.why: Large-format, Japanese-fusion dining is spreading beyond London, here into a large new leisure development rather than a high street.

news.headline: JNTO figures show British visits to Japan flat in August and up only 5.8% for the year so far.
news.body: Japan recorded 36,600 UK arrivals in August 2026, down 0.2% on August 2025, and 364,800 for January to August, up 5.8%. Total arrivals to Japan fell 9.6% in August, mainly because visitors from China dropped 59%.
news.why: After 22% growth in 2025, the UK market is slowing sharply, which matters for anyone planning capacity in Japan travel on last year's trend.

news.headline: The Pokémon Company says it will open a permanent Pokémon store in London by 2029.
news.body: It will be the brand's first permanent physical shop outside Asia and the first of several planned outside the region. No site has been announced; London has so far had only temporary Pokémon Center pop-ups.
news.why: A Japanese content owner is choosing London as its first permanent retail base outside Asia, a sign of how the UK fan market (lesson 15) is now valued directly by rights holders rather than only through licensees and events.

news.headline: Japan's visitor arrivals fell 5% in September to 3.10 million, but tourist spending rose.
news.body: Arrivals from China fell 44.5% to 430,800, while spending by visitors in July to September was an estimated ¥2.21 trillion, up 3.2%. January to September arrivals were 30.73 million, down 2.9%; the UK row of the September release was not in the coverage found.
news.why: With Chinese demand collapsing, Japan's tourism bodies lean harder on long-haul markets such as the UK, whose own growth slowed to 5.8% for January to August.

news.headline: Harvest season promoted across the vineyard routes.
news.body: Routes from Cappadocia and Çal to Urla and the newer Lidya Antik route ran harvest events, with travel agencies offering harvest tours.
news.why: Visits are one of the few legal ways for a winery to meet customers. The routes are growing in number.

news.headline: A leading Turkish wine writer says she no longer knows what she may post.
news.body: The writer behind The Quirky Cork said she is unsure whether branded photos or tasting notes are still allowed.
news.why: Bloggers and Instagram accounts were how people learned about new Turkish wines. That channel is now uncertain.

news.headline: An actor is fined for an alcohol brand in his personal posts.
news.body: Yiğit Dören was fined 82,244 lira after an alcohol brand appeared in his personal social media posts. He has appealed.
news.why: It shows personal accounts can be penalised, not only companies. The 2026 range for promotion offences is 103,207 to 4,130,222 lira. The court's decision on his appeal is the thing to watch.

news.headline: Parliament bars alcohol producers from sponsoring events under their brand.
news.body: The law stops producers, importers and marketers supporting any event with their brand, logo or company name, and restricts logos inside and outside business premises. The parts covering broadcasts and social media took effect on 20 June.
news.why: It closes most of the indirect routes wineries used after the 2013 ban, such as sponsored dinners and events.

news.headline: DNA testing shows the rare grape Kolorko is Hungary's Furmint.
news.body: Testing by the Paşaeli winery and the grape geneticist José Vouillamoz identified the Marmara grape Kolorko as Furmint. The same work matched Çal Karası to Crete's Liatiko.
news.why: The native-grape story is now being checked by science. Some "Turkish" grapes turn out to be shared with neighbours.

news.headline: The special consumption tax on wine rises 7.95%.
news.body: The fixed tax (ÖTV) on wine went from 56.87 to 61.39 lira.
news.why: The tax is updated every January and July in line with producer prices, so shelf prices rise on a fixed timetable.

news.headline: Turkey's national viticulture symposium met in Tekirdağ, with native grapes and heat stress high on the agenda.
news.body: The 11th Turkish Viticulture and Technologies Symposium, hosted by the Tekirdağ Viticulture Research Institute with guests from Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Bulgaria, heard papers on Öküzgözü from five Elazığ sites, Papazkarası wine yeasts, Kalecik Karası clones and protecting grapes from sunburn. A researcher from the institute said two Thracian producers are close to releasing wine from the revived Karamenüş grape; the next symposium is in Diyarbakır in 2030.
news.why: It shows where state-backed grape research is heading: native varieties, local yeasts and adapting vineyards to heat. A speaker also named the lack of wine-tourism policy as the main obstacle to that income stream.

news.headline: The agriculture minister forecast a 2026 grape crop of about 3.85 million tonnes, up from about 2.5 million in 2025.
news.body: Speaking at a harvest event in Kalecik, Ankara, İbrahim Yumaklı called 2026 the wettest year in 66 years. TÜİK's first crop estimate in May had already pointed to a 53% rise in grape production.
news.why: After the poor 2025 crop, a large harvest should ease grape supply and prices for wineries that buy fruit. Most of the crop is table and drying grapes, so the effect on wine grapes specifically is not stated.
